title: Inherited Property I Don't Want: How to Sell Fast and Move On
excerpt: Inheriting a property sounds like good news, but it can quickly become a financial and emotional burden. Here's exactly how to sell an unwanted inherited property fast — and walk away with cash in hand.
author: AIWholesail Team

metaDescription: Inherited property you don't want? Learn how to sell fast with probate tips, cash buyer strategies, and step-by-step guidance to close quickly.

sections.content: You just inherited a house. Maybe it belonged to a parent, grandparent, or a distant relative you barely knew. And now, instead of feeling relieved, you're staring down property taxes, maintenance bills, and a house you don't want — possibly hundreds of miles away. If you're thinking 'I inherited property I don't want and need to know how to sell fast,' you're not alone. Thousands of Americans find themselves in this exact situation every year, and the good news is there are clear, proven ways to turn that unwanted property into cash quickly.
Understanding What You're Actually Dealing With

Before you list the home or call a cash buyer, you need to understand exactly what you own — and what strings are attached. Inherited properties often come with complications that regular home sales don't. These include outstanding mortgages, back taxes, liens, or deferred maintenance. In some cases, multiple heirs are involved, which means everyone needs to agree before anything can be sold. Taking stock of the full picture upfront saves you from nasty surprises down the road.

items: Get a copy of the death certificate and the will (or trust documents) as soon as possible
Check if the property is in probate — this affects your timeline significantly
Order a title search to uncover any liens, back taxes, or outstanding mortgages
Find out if other heirs have a legal claim to the property
Get a rough idea of the home's current market value before making any decisions

sections.content: The Probate Question: Does It Apply to You?

Probate is the legal process of validating a will and transferring ownership of assets. If the property is still in the deceased person's name and wasn't held in a trust, it likely needs to go through probate before you can sell it. In some states, probate can take 6 to 12 months. In others, simplified processes exist for smaller estates. For example, in Texas — one of the busier markets for inherited homes — there is an 'independent administration' option that can speed things up considerably. If you're in a fast-moving market like [Dallas](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/dallas-tx) or [Atlanta](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/atlanta-ga), every month you wait costs you holding expenses like taxes, insurance, and utilities.

Pro Tip: Hire a probate attorney early. A consultation typically costs $150 to $300, but the guidance can save you months of delays and thousands in avoidable costs. Many offer free initial consultations.
Your 3 Main Options to Sell an Inherited Property Fast
Option 1: Sell to a Cash Buyer or Real Estate Investor

This is the fastest route. Cash buyers — often real estate investors or wholesalers — can close in as little as 7 to 14 days. They buy properties as-is, which means you don't need to repair the leaking roof or replace the 30-year-old HVAC system. The trade-off is that you'll typically receive 65% to 80% of the home's after-repair value (ARV). On a home with a $250,000 ARV that needs $40,000 in repairs, a cash buyer might offer $130,000 to $160,000. That sounds low, but when you factor in agent commissions, holding costs, and repair bills on a traditional sale, the difference can shrink dramatically.
Option 2: List with a Traditional Real Estate Agent

If maximizing sale price is more important than speed, listing on the MLS with an experienced agent is worth considering. In a hot market like [Phoenix](https://aiwholesail.com/markets/phoenix-az), well-priced inherited homes can sell in under 30 days. However, you'll need to budget for agent commissions (typically 5% to 6%), potential repairs, staging, and carrying costs during the listing period. This option works best when the home is in decent shape and probate has already been completed.
Option 3: Wholesale the Property

Wholesaling is a middle-ground option many people overlook. In a wholesale deal, you sign a purchase contract with a buyer who then assigns that contract to an end investor for a fee. You still get a quick, cash-based close — often within 2 to 3 weeks — without having to list the home publicly. Wholesalers handle the marketing and find the end buyer for you. This approach works especially well for distressed properties in markets like Atlanta where investor demand is high. If you're curious how wholesaling works from the other side of the transaction, the [Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners guide](https://aiwholesail.com/guides/wholesaling-real-estate-for-beginners) breaks it down step by step.
How to Price an Inherited Property Accurately

Pricing is the most critical factor in selling quickly. Price too high and the home sits. Price too low and you leave money on the table. A comparative market analysis (CMA) from a local agent is a good starting point, but it helps to run your own numbers too. Look at recent sales of similar homes within a half-mile radius and adjust for condition, size, and upgrades. For inherited homes that need work, you'll want to calculate both the as-is value and the after-repair value, then decide which selling path makes the most financial sense. Use the free [Deal Calculator at AIWholesail](https://aiwholesail.com/tools/wholesale-deal-calculator) to quickly model your numbers and see what a realistic cash offer should look like before you start taking calls from buyers.

'The biggest mistake heirs make is waiting too long. Every month a vacant property sits costs money — taxes, insurance, utilities, and depreciation. Speed is often worth more than squeezing out an extra $5,000 on the sale price.' — Experienced probate real estate attorney
Tax Implications You Should Know Before You Sell

One of the best-kept secrets in inherited real estate is the stepped-up cost basis. When you inherit a property, the IRS resets the cost basis to the home's fair market value at the time of the original owner's death — not what they paid for it decades ago. This means if your relative paid $60,000 for the home in 1985, and it's worth $280,000 today, your basis is $280,000. If you sell quickly for $275,000, you may owe little to no capital gains tax. This is a massive financial advantage, and it's one of the strongest reasons to sell sooner rather than later. Always consult a CPA or tax advisor to confirm your specific situation before closing.
Step-by-Step Action Plan to Sell Your Inherited Property Fast

items: Step 1: Confirm legal ownership — get the will, trust documents, and death certificate in order
Step 2: Determine if probate is required and hire a probate attorney if needed
Step 3: Order a title search to find any liens, back taxes, or encumbrances
Step 4: Get a professional appraisal or CMA to establish market value
Step 5: Run your numbers using an online deal calculator to evaluate cash offer vs. traditional sale
Step 6: Reach out to at least 3 to 5 cash buyers or investors for competing offers
Step 7: Choose your selling method — cash buyer, agent listing, or wholesale deal
Step 8: Review offers carefully with a real estate attorney before signing anything
Step 9: Close the deal and transfer title — then handle final tax filing with your CPA

sections.content: Pro Tip: Don't throw anything away before closing. Old items in the home — antique furniture, jewelry, collectibles — could have significant value. Hire an estate sale company to assess contents before clearing the property. Many work on commission with no upfront cost.
Common Mistakes That Slow Down the Sale

Heirs who try to handle everything on their own often run into avoidable delays. Skipping the title search, accepting the first offer without comparing alternatives, or making expensive repairs before understanding buyer demand can all cost you time and money. If multiple heirs are involved, get a written agreement in place early — disputes between family members are one of the top reasons inherited property sales fall apart.
